definition: The ugly duckling theorem is an argument showing that classification is not really possible without some sort of bias.
details: More particularly, it assumes finitely many properties combinable by logical connectives, and finitely many objects; it asserts that any two different objects share the same number of (extensional) properties. The theorem is named after Hans Christian Andersen's 1843 story "The Ugly Duckling", because it shows that a duckling is just as similar to a swan as two swans are to each other. It was derived by Satosi Watanabe in 1969.

explainer.lead: The ugly duckling theorem argues that classification is not really possible without some sort of bias. It matters because it shows similarity alone cannot decide categories.

tiers.eli5: Like saying a duckling is just as similar to a swan as two swans are to each other, so without a preference you cannot group them.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers cite it to justify why models need inductive bias rather than raw feature matching; a pitfall is assuming a feature set alone will separate classes without bias.

explainer.example: Under the theorem, a duckling shares as many properties with a swan as two swans share with each other, so classification requires added bias.
